title: Checkpoint: The Ides of March
objective: After this level you can explain Caesar’s dictatorship, his assassination, and why the Republic still did not survive.
summary: Made dictator for life in 44 BCE, Caesar was killed on the Ides of March. The plotters wanted the Republic back; they got more war.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale. Beware the Ides of March.
cards.body: How a century of crisis ended with a murder in the Senate.

cards.headline: Dictator for life
cards.body: After his victory in the civil war, Caesar was made dictator in 44 BCE, and then dictator for life. To many senators this looked like the kingship Rome had sworn never to allow again.

cards.headline: The Ides of March
cards.body: On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, Caesar was stabbed to death at a meeting of the Senate. The conspirators were led by Brutus and Cassius. Brutus claimed descent from the Brutus who had expelled Rome’s last king. They hoped to restore the Republic, but Caesar’s murder only led to more civil war.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: Caesar was made dictator for life in 44 BCE
He was killed on 15 March 44 BCE
Brutus and Cassius led the plot
The murder brought more civil war

questions.prompt: On what date was Julius Caesar assassinated?

options.label: 1 January 49 BCE
27 BCE
options.rationale: That’s the start of the Empire.

options.label: 15 March 44 BCE
9 August 48 BCE

questions.explanation: Caesar was killed on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE.

questions.prompt: Which general first marched on Rome with his army?

options.label: Julius Caesar
Pompey
options.rationale: He didn’t march on Rome first.

options.label: Sulla
Marius
options.rationale: Sulla did it first, in 88 BCE.

questions.explanation: Sulla marched on Rome in 88 BCE, the precedent Caesar followed.

questions.prompt: Why did “dictator for life” alarm so many senators?

options.label: It looked like the kingship Rome had sworn off
It meant Caesar would leave Rome for good
It gave power to the tribunes
options.rationale: It gave power to one man.

options.label: It had never been tried in Gaul

questions.explanation: A dictatorship without end looked like monarchy, which Romans had rejected since 509 BCE.

questions.prompt: What did Marius’s reforms and Caesar’s conquest of Gaul have in common?

options.label: Both weakened the Roman army
Both brought the Punic Wars to an end
Both gave land to the Gauls
Both built armies loyal to a general

questions.explanation: Soldiers who depended on their commander made generals like Caesar powerful enough to defy the Senate.

questions.prompt: Chapter 4 recap: why didn’t killing Caesar save the Republic?

options.label: The Senate crowned Caesar’s son as king
Loyal armies and violence had replaced votes
Carthage invaded Italy during the chaos
Caesar had abolished the Senate

questions.explanation: Since the Gracchi, disputes had been settled by force, and armies followed generals; murder brought war, not the old Republic.
